title: That time of year: the three images
short: Three quatrains present the ageing speaker as late autumn, twilight, and a dying fire: the timescale shrinks from a year to a day to an hour.
body: Each quatrain offers a new metaphor for the speaker's age, introduced by a variation on 'thou mayst in me behold' / 'In me thou see'st'. The images run from a season (late autumn) to a day (twilight) to a single fire burning down, so that the time left grows shorter in each, and the images become more intimate. Vendler and others note the increasing sense of enclosure: open woods, then the closing night, then the fire smothered in its own ashes. The addressee is made a spectator ('behold', 'see'st', 'perceiv'st'), which prepares the couplet's turn to the beloved's response.

anchor: yellow leaves, or none, or few
title: yellow leaves, or none, or few
short: Autumn leaves, with the order of the list correcting itself: the speaker hesitates over how bare the tree is.
body: Yellow leaves are a conventional sign of old age; compare Macbeth 5.3, 'my way of life / Is fall'n into the sere, the yellow leaf'. The odd order of the series, 'yellow leaves, or none, or few', is expressive: the speaker first says some leaves remain, then that none do, then corrects himself to 'few', as though unwilling to admit or to exaggerate his decline. Booth discusses the line as an example of the sonnet's hesitant, self-qualifying movement.

title: Bare ruin'd choirs
short: The bare branches resemble the ruined choirs of churches, where birds once sang as choristers did; the Quarto prints 'rn'wd quiers'.
body: The 'choir' (spelled quire in the period) is the part of a church where the singers sat. The branches, bare of leaves, are like the roofless choirs of ruined churches, and the birds that sang there are like choristers. Many commentators connect the image with the abbeys and monastic churches left to decay after Henry VIII's dissolution of the monasteries (1536-41), a familiar sight in Shakespeare's England; others think this is reading in too much. William Empson's Seven Types of Ambiguity (1930) made the line a famous example of meaning that works through many associations at once (carved wood, singing, the shelter of the church) without one being primary. The 1609 Quarto reads 'Bare rn'wd quiers', which is universally emended to 'ruin'd choirs'.

title: where late the sweet birds sang
short: Lately the birds sang there; the singers are both birds and choristers, and perhaps the poet's own younger voice.
body: 'Late' means lately, recently. The birds who sang in summer have gone, as choirboys have gone from ruined churches. Many readers see a further application to the poet: his own song (his poetry) belongs to a past season. The line's slow, heavy monosyllables, with stresses crowded together in 'Bare ruin'd choirs', contrast with the lighter close 'where late the sweet birds sang', so that the sound itself moves from desolation to memory.

title: twilight
short: The second image: the dim light left after sunset, a shorter span than the autumn of the first quatrain.
body: The second quatrain moves from the year to the day. Twilight is the faint light lingering in the west after sunset, the last remainder of a day that is already over. The archaic verb 'fadeth' slows the line. As with the autumn tree, the speaker presents himself not as dead but as near the end, a remnant of something already past its prime.

title: by and by
short: Soon, before long (not 'eventually'): night will very shortly take the twilight away.
body: In Elizabethan English 'by and by' usually meant 'immediately' or 'very soon' (OED 'by and by' adv., sense 2), a stronger sense than its later meaning 'eventually'. The phrase stresses how little time remains between twilight and full dark. Shakespeare often uses it in this urgent sense in the plays, where a character promises to come 'by and by', meaning at once. Read with the modern sense, the line would lose its pressure: the quatrain moves from fading light to its sudden removal, and the black night that 'doth take away' the twilight arrives almost as soon as it is mentioned, which is the point of the speaker's warning about his own short time.

title: Death's second self
short: Night (or sleep) is death's double: an ancient idea, since in Greek myth Sleep and Death are twin brothers, children of Night.
body: A 'second self' is a double or alter ego. Night is Death's second self because it brings darkness and rest that resemble death, and because it brings sleep, traditionally Death's twin. In Hesiod's Theogony (211-12, 756-66) Night gives birth to Sleep (Hypnos) and Death (Thanatos), and in the Iliad (16.672, 682) Sleep and Death are twin brothers who carry away the body of Sarpedon. The idea was a Renaissance commonplace (Samuel Daniel calls sleep 'brother to Death' in Delia). The phrase prepares the darker reference to 'death-bed' in line 11.

title: seals up
short: Closes up, encloses everything in rest, as eyes are closed in sleep or death and a document is sealed.
body: To 'seal up' is to close firmly, as a letter or a tomb is sealed, and also to close the eyes in sleep or death. 'All' extends the darkness to the whole world. The language of sealing appears elsewhere in Shakespeare for night's closing of the eyes, and the same word could be spelled like 'seel', the falconer's term for sewing up a hawk's eyelids (compare Macbeth 3.2, 'Come, seeling night'), a resonance some readers hear here.

title: the glowing of such fire
short: The third image: embers glowing on the ashes of what has already burned, the shortest timescale of all.
body: The third quatrain is the most intimate and the most complex. The speaker is not a blazing fire but the glow of embers lying on 'the ashes of his youth', that is, the fire's (his = its) own earlier fuel. Youth has become the ash on which age now lies. The image of life as a flame was traditional, and Shakespeare's Sonnet 1 already speaks of the youth feeding 'thy light's flame with self-substantial fuel'.

title: his youth
short: 'His' means 'its' (the fire's): the burnt-out remains of the fire's earlier blaze, standing for the speaker's youth.
body: 'Its' was only just entering English in Shakespeare's time, and 'his' was the normal neuter possessive (OED 'his' pron.). The 'ashes of his youth' are the fire's own burnt fuel; the glow lies on them as on a bed. Since the fire represents the speaker, the line also says that his youth has been consumed and now lies under him. The bed image leads directly into 'death-bed' in the next line.

title: death-bed
short: The ashes are the deathbed on which the fire must 'expire' (both 'die' and 'breathe out').
body: The ashes become 'the death-bed, whereon it must expire'. 'Expire' means both to die and, in its Latin root (exspirare), to breathe out, so the fire's last breath is also a dying man's. The image of a deathbed brings the poem closest to literal death; the first two quatrains spoke of seasons and of night, but this one names the bed on which a person dies.

anchor: Consum'd with that which it was nourish'd by
title: Consum'd with that which it was nourish'd by
short: A paradox: the fire is choked by the ashes of the fuel that once fed it, as life is used up by the very process of living.
body: The line's paradox is that what once nourished the fire (its fuel) now, as ash, smothers it. 'With' can mean 'by' or 'along with', so the fire is consumed by its fuel and together with it. Renaissance emblem culture expressed the idea in the Latin motto 'Quod me nutrit me destruit' ('what nourishes me destroys me'), which appears on the portrait at Corpus Christi College, Cambridge, often thought to be of Christopher Marlowe (1585). Applied to the speaker, the line suggests that the passions or energies that sustained his life are what wear it away. Compare Sonnet 1, 'Feed'st thy light's flame with self-substantial fuel'.

title: the couplet: love that well, which thou must leave
short: Seeing the speaker's age makes the beloved's love stronger; but 'that' and 'leave' are ambiguous, and critics read the couplet differently.
body: The couplet turns from the speaker to the addressee. On the common reading, perceiving the speaker's age makes the friend love him more strongly, because he must soon lose him: 'leave' means 'lose' or 'part from'. But 'that which thou must leave ere long' could instead be the friend's own youth, which he too must give up, so the poem would warn him to value his own life. Some critics (Booth among them) find the couplet less confident than it sounds: the speaker may be hoping, even pleading, rather than describing the friend's feelings. 'This' gathers up all three images.
